title: Find the commit that broke it with bisect

scenario.brief:
Invoices are showing unrounded tax again — `7.4999999` instead of `7.50`. It worked a week ago, somewhere in the last several commits it broke, and nobody remembers which change did it. Reading every diff by hand would take ages.

`git bisect` finds the culprit by binary search. You tell it one commit that's **good** (the version from a week ago) and one that's **bad** (now). It checks out the midpoint; you test and tell it `good` or `bad`; it halves the range each time until one commit remains — the first bad commit.

**Approach.**

1. Start: `git bisect start HEAD HEAD~6` (HEAD is bad, HEAD~6 is the last known-good build).
2. At each step Git checks out a commit. Look at `src/tax.js`: if it rounds (`Math.round`), it's `git bisect good`; if not, `git bisect bad`.
3. When Git prints "… is the first bad commit", that's your culprit. Run `git bisect reset` to return, then write the bad commit's short id and the reason into `ANSWERS.md`.
scenario.whyItMatters: On a long history, bisect turns "when did this break?" from an afternoon of guessing into a handful of tests — O(log n) instead of O(n). It's the fastest way to localize a regression, and knowing it is a mark of someone who debugs methodically.

files.src/invoice.js:
const { tax } = require('./tax')
module.exports = { grandTotal: (s) => s + tax(s) }

objectives.title: Record the first bad commit in ANSWERS.md
objectives.description: Write the short id of the commit that dropped the rounding.
hints: Run the bisect: `git bisect start HEAD HEAD~6`, then mark each checked-out commit `good` (tax.js rounds) or `bad` (it doesn't).
When Git says "… is the first bad commit", copy that short id.
`git bisect reset`, then `echo "Bad commit: <short id> — dropped Math.round" > ANSWERS.md`.

objectives.title: Note why it's the bug
hints: A good bisect finding says what the commit did wrong, not just its id.
The culprit removed the rounding from the tax calculation.
Add a short reason to ANSWERS.md, e.g. 'dropped Math.round from tax()'.

debrief.summary: You localized a regression with git bisect — a binary search over history — instead of reading every commit, and recorded which change introduced it.
internals: Bisect keeps a set of suspects: commits reachable from the bad commit but not from any good one.
Each `good`/`bad` you give halves that set; Git checks out the midpoint for you to test next.
When one suspect remains, it's reported as the first bad commit — the earliest commit where the bug is present.
Bisect checks commits out in a detached HEAD; `git bisect reset` returns you to where you started.

keyCommands.note: Begin; give a known-bad and known-good commit.
End the bisect and return to your branch.

commonMistakes: Swapping good and bad, so bisect reports a nonsense result.
Testing the wrong thing at each step — be consistent about what 'bad' means.
Forgetting `git bisect reset`, leaving yourself on a detached HEAD.
debrief.atWork: When a regression slips in and the history is long, bisect is the professional reflex: pick a known-good point, a known-bad point, and let binary search find the commit in a few steps. With a scripted test, `git bisect run` automates even that.
debrief.interview: "How do you find which commit introduced a bug?" Answer: git bisect — mark a good and bad commit and binary-search, testing the midpoint each step, until it names the first bad commit.

solution: echo "Bad commit: {{label:regression:short}} — dropped Math.round from tax()" > ANSWERS.md
